newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israelis, Palestinians set to resume peace talks.
newsitem.headline: Israelis, Palestinians set to resume peace talks.

text.p: Israelis and Palestinians were set to resume peace talks on Sunday, with a threat of renewed violence in the West Bank and Gaza Strip looming over them if negotiations failed.
U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher will meet Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Palestinian President Yasser Arafat separately ahead of the talks, officials said.

Members of the joint Israeli-Palestinian steering committee were scheduled to meet at the Erez crossing between Israel and Gaza at 6 p.m. (1600 GMT) to hammer out differences over agreements reached with Israel's previous government.

"We will not renegotiate or reopen agreements signed. We will not agree to modifications of agreements signed," Palestinian negotiator Saeb Erekat told reporters. But Israel has said it wants to do just that.
Erekat was speaking after Arafat briefed members of his Palestinian self-rule Authority in Gaza on Saturday on results of an emergency Washington peace summit with Netanyahu.

U.S. President Bill Clinton convened the meeting because of the crisis caused by Israeli-Palestinian clashes that killed 73 people after Israel opened a new entrance to an archaeological tunnel near a Moslem shrine in Jerusalem's Old City.

The violence, the most serious since Israel and the Palestine Liberation Organisation reached a landmark peace deal in 1993, reflected months of Palestinian frustration at slow pace of subsequent negotiations.
Israeli hardliners hailed Netanyahu for refusing to give any concessions to Arafat in Washington on the tunnel issue or set a date for Israel's promised redeployment of troops in Hebron.
The fate of Hebron, the last big West Bank town under Israeli occupation and the only one with a Jewish settler population, was expected to head the agenda at Sunday's meeting.
"There's no timetable (for a withdrawal from Hebron). I can't say how long," said Israeli Defence Minister Yitzhak Mordechai in remarks broadcast on Israel Television.

Israel had agreed to leave parts of Hebron by last March but postponed a withdrawal after Islamic suicide bombers killed 59 people in the Jewish state. It now wants better arrangements to safeguard the 400 Jews living among 100,000 Palestinians there.
Thousands of religious Jews celebrating the Jewish Simha Torah feast in Hebron demanded that Israel must never withdraw from the town, which is holy to both Moslems and Jews.

In Jerusalem, thousands of Israelis took to the streets to protest at Netanyahu's handling of Middle East peace talks and to mourn prime minister Yitzhak Rabin, shot dead 11 months ago by a right-wing Israeli angered by his peace policies.
"We did not come here to hate," Rabin's son, Yuval, told the crowd. "We came here to remember..."
